clue.text: Savoy opera led hero to sing out

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of led hero to sing are put out of order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A Savoy opera begins with the leading man bursting into song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' turns the thirteen letters of LED HERO TO SING into the title. The Savoy operas are the Gilbert and Sullivan works first staged at London's Savoy Theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the Gilbert and Sullivan comic operas staged by the D'Oyly Carte company at the Savoy Theatre.

clue.text: What to do about cold girl, Erica?

parts.note: the remedy for being cold is to warm things up, so heat
her stands for a girl or woman, as a pronoun

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about how to help a chilly girl called Erica.
explanation.walkthrough: Erica looks like the girl's name, but it is the botanical genus of the plant, so it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the Latin genus name for the low moorland shrub with purple bell flowers.

clue.text: This painter had to proceed by half a yard

parts.note: to proceed is to go on

indicators.note: half a takes the first two of the four letters of yard

explanation.surface: An artist has to make progress by a short distance at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half a' takes the front half of the four-letter word, and 'had to' and 'by' are only joining words in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Francisco Goya was the Spanish court painter of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

clue.text: Court-divider depends on it

parts.note: the tennis net that divides the court hangs from a tensioned line along its top

explanation.surface: Something vital to whatever splits a court in two.
explanation.walkthrough: The net that divides a tennis court is held up by a cord along its top, and a serve that clips the top of the net is also called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The cable strung along the top of a tennis net, which keeps it taut, is named after it.

clue.text: Heart of Midlothian he'll love in play …

indicators.note: heart of picks the central two letters of the ten in Midlothian

parts.note: he'll, with the apostrophe dropped, gives the letters hell
love is nil in tennis scoring, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A football reference: someone from Hearts of Midlothian says he'll love going to a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart of' takes OT from the middle of MIDLOTHIAN; Heart of Midlothian is also an Edinburgh football club, which hides the device.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy of the Moor of Venice and his jealousy is a stage drama.

clue.text: … club of mettle, we hear

explanation.surface: Continuing from the play, a weapon for a spirited man.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is heard: 'of mettle' said out loud is 'of metal', which describes something made of this element.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf club with a metal head has this name, and the adjective means made of metal, which 'of mettle' sounds like.

clue.text: Paler getting up, not quite set-setback for patient

indicators.note: in a down clue getting up means the word paler is read from bottom to top
not quite means the word set loses its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone looking paler, not quite set, has a setback after illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting up' turns PALER into RELAP in this down clue; 'not quite' cuts SET to SE.
explanation.definitionFit: A relapse is the return of an illness after a patient seemed to be recovering.

clue.text: Dilutes rose fruit the rabbity way

annotationWithheld.why: Dilutes rose fruit the rabbity way (9,4): WATERS (dilutes) + HIP (rose fruit) gives WATERSHIP, but nothing but 'way', which is also part of the definition 'the rabbity way', supplies DOWN; a word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Dilutes rose fruit the rabbity way

clue.text: Ellen Smith, MBE, excited, shows decoration

indicators.note: excited suggests the letters are stirred up into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman called Ellen Smith, newly made an MBE, proudly shows off her honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' rearranges the letters of ELLEN SMITH and MBE. An MBE (Member of the Order of the British Empire) is a British honour, which makes 'decoration' look like the medal.
explanation.definitionFit: Embellishment is ornament added to make something more attractive, which is decoration.

clue.text: Minds his business?

parts.note: reads as a polite person keeping to himself, but describes a psychiatrist whose trade is other people's minds

explanation.surface: A man who keeps himself to himself.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'minds his own business' is turned round: for this professional, minds are the business.
explanation.definitionFit: A psychoanalyst, often shortened to this, treats the mental life of patients.

clue.text: Putting cowl on chimney is criminal

indicators.note: in an across clue on puts the first piece before the next, so cowl comes first

parts.note: a cowl is a monk's hood
lum is the Scots word for a chimney

explanation.surface: Fitting a cowl to the top of a chimney is a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: LUM is the Scottish word for chimney. A chimney cowl is a real fitting, which makes the surface read as roofing.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoodlum is a violent thug or gangster, so a criminal.

clue.text: Reverberation in part of the chorus

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A ringing sound carries through a section of the choir.
explanation.definitionFit: An echo is a sound reflected back, a reverberation.

clue.text: Guys preceded them on Broadway

parts.note: refers to the title of a Broadway musical in which the word Guys comes first and these come after

explanation.surface: Men went ahead of some women along a New York street.
explanation.walkthrough: The musical 'Guys and ...' opened on Broadway in 1950; in its title the guys come first.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for attractive young women, as in the Frank Loesser musical title that pairs them with guys.

clue.text: What's the point of fencing?

parts.note: seems to question why anyone fences, but asks which sword is used, its point being what scores

explanation.surface: Someone asking why anybody bothers with the sport of swordplay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'point' means both purpose and the sharp tip; in this weapon's discipline only hits with the tip count.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the fencing sword with a stiff blade on which touches are scored only with its tip.

clue.text: Yarn preserved by many longshoremen

indicators.note: preserved by means the answer is kept inside the run of letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A thread or story kept alive by dockworkers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yarn' tempts as a sailor's tale told by the longshoremen; it is the thread.
explanation.definitionFit: Nylon is a synthetic fibre spun into thread, so a kind of yarn.

clue.text: Very light, for example

parts.note: Very here is a proper name, Edward Very, who gave his name to a coloured signal shot from a pistol

explanation.surface: Something extremely pale or weighing almost nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: A Very light is a signal flare fired from a Very pistol, named after its American inventor; 'Very' looks like the adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: A Very light is one type of signal rocket fired at sea or in war to give a bright burst of light.

clue.text: Deary, perhaps, on street fell from virtue

indicators.note: perhaps hints the word Deary may be something else, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone affectionately called Deary went on the streets and lost their good name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' says the name is to be rearranged; 'on' sets it after the street abbreviation. 'fell' looks like the past of fall but completes 'fell from virtue'.
explanation.definitionFit: To have strayed is to have wandered off the right path, morally lapsed.

clue.text: Leo will turn into a gusher

indicators.note: turn into means the letters of Leo will are turned into something new

explanation.surface: A man called Leo will become an excitable talker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn' rearranges the letters of LEO WILL; 'gusher' looks like a person who gushes.
explanation.definitionFit: A gusher is a well from which oil spurts up under its own pressure.

clue.text: Not out India's openers attract gates

parts.note: the opening two letters of India
gates and doors are both ways in that open and shut

explanation.surface: A cricket picture: India's opening batsmen, still not out, draw crowds through the gates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not out' is a cricket term for a batsman still in, but here it simply means inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inside a building is the opposite of being outside.

clue.text: Stiff drinks served at Wimbledon

explanation.surface: Strong spirits handed out at the tennis championships.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon is the London tennis championship, where pairs play each other in this format.
explanation.definitionFit: A double measure of spirits is a stiff drink, and tennis played two against two is the pairs game.

clue.text: Psst! cue gone wrong for murder-mystery figure

indicators.note: gone wrong suggests letters that have been knocked out of their proper order

explanation.surface: An actor's whispered prompt goes astray in a whodunit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone wrong' rearranges the letters of PSST and CUE.
explanation.definitionFit: In a detective story the people under suspicion of the murder are the characters the reader tries to pick between.

clue.text: Looks around jumble-sale and for how long?

explanation.surface: Someone browses a charity sale and wonders how much time it will take.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is an answer to its question: asked 'how long?', one may say a very long time, which read as two words gives the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To rummage through goods searching for something is to hunt about, and a reply to 'how long?' can be 'a very long time'.

clue.text: Female on Scottish river-she's come from Florence

indicators.note: in a down clue on puts the first piece above the next, so female comes first

parts.note: the Lossie is a river in Moray, north-east Scotland, reaching the sea at Lossiemouth

explanation.surface: A woman from Italy settles beside a river in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from Florence' looks like the Italian city but means the girl's name, from which this pet form derives.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a traditional pet form of the girl's name Florence.

clue.text: Adult Greek to confess

parts.note: to confess is to own up

explanation.surface: A Greek grown man has to admit everything.
explanation.definitionFit: A fully mature person, no longer a child, is called by this informal term.

clue.text: Ridge of high pressure?

parts.note: reads as weather-map language, but describes a hill ridge, and a taut skin beaten for sound, kept under high tension

explanation.surface: A forecaster's phrase for an elongated area of high air pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'ridge of high pressure' is a weather term. In Scotland and Ireland a long narrow hill is known by this name, and the musical instrument has a skin stretched under tension.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scottish and Irish place names a long low hill is called by this word, as in drumlin, and the instrument's skin is kept taut.

clue.text: First capital gains tax in Berkshire

parts.note: the first capital letter of the alphabet
scot is an old word for a tax, surviving in scot-free

explanation.surface: Berkshire is the first place to see a capital gains tax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital gains tax' reads as one phrase but splits: 'gains' joins A to SCOT, the old tax of 'scot-free'.
explanation.definitionFit: The town known for its racecourse lies in the county of Berkshire, west of London.

clue.text: Space for 5 in retirement

indicators.note: in retirement means going backwards, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: the title character of 5-down is called the Moor of Venice

explanation.surface: A place for a retired person to live.
explanation.walkthrough: '5' points to 5-down, whose hero is a Moor; 'in retirement' reads MOOR backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Room means available area or space, as in 'no room to move'.

clue.text: Be mother for the French

explanation.surface: Someone serves the tea for the French guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Be mother' is British slang for pouring out the tea; the French word for 'for' has the same letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To be mother is to serve the tea from the pot, and the French preposition meaning 'for' is spelt the same way.

clue.text: Long-distance ring 8 chancy game

parts.note: far means a long way off
a ring is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: Telephoning far away for a game of chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' looks like a phone call, but it is the O shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Faro is an old gambling card game in which players bet on the order cards are dealt.

clue.text: Kind of mat worn out by prolonged sitting?

explanation.surface: A doormat wears thin after people stand on it for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition uses 'outstay your welcome': a guest who sits on too long wears out the hospitality.
explanation.definitionFit: A doormat at the front door is a common type, and a guest staying too long uses up the friendly reception.

clue.text: Currently part of Limerick

parts.note: Currently means as a flowing current, so a river passing through the Irish city and county

explanation.surface: Something that belongs to the Irish county at present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currently' seems to mean 'at present' but means in the form of a flowing current: Ireland's longest river runs through Limerick.
explanation.definitionFit: Ireland's longest river flows through Limerick city to its estuary.

clue.text: Care for the body

parts.note: reads as looking after one's physical health, but means the loyal spirit felt for a group, a body of people

explanation.surface: Advice about looking after one's physical health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body' looks like the physical frame but means a body of people; the French phrase means spirit of the group.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase for team spirit names the morale and loyalty members feel toward their group.
